title: Data Hazards in PIPE: Forwarding, Stalling and Bubbles

sections.heading: RAW Hazards in a Five-Stage Pipeline
sections.body:
PIPE, the pipelined Y86-64 implementation in CS:APP, splits instruction processing into five stages — Fetch (F), Decode (D), Execute (E), Memory (M) and Write-back (W) — so that five instructions are in flight at once, each one stage behind the previous one. This is only correct if the pipeline produces exactly the results a sequential (one-instruction-at-a-time) execution would. The invariant that can break is a **read-after-write (RAW) data hazard**: an instruction in D needs the value of a register that an earlier, still in-flight instruction has not yet written back.

In Y86-64, a register's architectural value is defined to update at the end of the cycle in which its producer is in stage W. Decode happens up to three stages earlier than Write-back for an in-flight neighbor, so if the consumer reads the register file directly in D, it can see a **stale** value — the one from before the producer's update — while an instruction three or four positions behind it in program order correctly sees the new one. The fix is not to slow the pipeline down in the common case; it is to detect, cycle by cycle, which of the three producer stages (E, M, W) currently holds a value destined for one of the two source registers `d_srcA`/`d_srcB` of the instruction in D, and route that value directly into Decode instead of the (possibly stale) register-file read. This mechanism is **forwarding**, and it resolves every RAW hazard in PIPE except one, discussed below.

sections.heading: Forwarding: Priority Among E, M and W
sections.body:
PIPE's decode stage has a dedicated block (CS:APP calls it "Sel+Fwd A" for `valA`, "Fwd B" for `valB`) that compares the two source register IDs against the destination IDs carried by the E, M and W pipeline registers, and selects whichever forwarded value matches — falling back to the register file only if none does. The actual priority chain for `valA`, transcribed from the CENG331 PIPE slides, is:

```text
int d_valA = [
    D_icode in { ICALL, IJXX } : D_valP;     # use incremented PC, not a hazard case
    d_srcA == e_dstE           : e_valE;     # forward valE from Execute (freshest)
    d_srcA == M_dstM           : m_valM;     # forward valM from Memory (just read)
    d_srcA == M_dstE           : M_valE;     # forward valE from Memory
    d_srcA == W_dstM           : W_valM;     # forward valM from Write-back
    d_srcA == W_dstE           : W_valE;     # forward valE from Write-back
    1                          : d_rvalA;    # no match: use the register file
];
```

`valB` is selected the same way against `d_srcB`. The order is not arbitrary: if two in-flight producers both target the same register, the one **closer to Decode** is the one more recent in program order, so it must win. An instruction in E was fetched after the one in M, which was fetched after the one in W; picking a later entry in the list over an earlier match would forward a value that a more recent instruction is about to overwrite. Lower-case names (`e_valE`, `m_valM`) are the real-time signals computed combinationally *within* a stage this cycle, before being latched; upper-case names (`M_valE`, `W_dstM`, …) are values already sitting in a pipeline register from a previous cycle. The `M_dstM`/`m_valM` and `W_dstM`/`W_valM` rows exist because a load's result is not available until its producer sits in M or W — which is exactly where forwarding runs out of road.

sections.heading: The Load/Use Hazard
sections.body:
One dependency this chain cannot satisfy: the destination of a load (`mrmovq` or `popq`) is not known until the *end* of that instruction's Memory stage, because the data has to come back from the memory system. If the very next instruction needs that value, it reaches Decode one full cycle before the load reaches Memory — the forwarding logic would have to send a value backward in time, which is impossible. CS:APP's canonical example has `mrmovq 0(%rdx),%rax` followed immediately by `addq %rbx,%rax`: the `addq` needs `%rax` in Decode at the same cycle the `mrmovq` is still sitting in Execute, one stage short of producing it.

The detection condition, read directly off the PIPE control logic, is

```text
bool load_use_hazard =
    E_icode in { IMRMOVQ, IPOPQ } && E_dstM in { d_srcA, d_srcB };
```

— the instruction currently in E is a load, and its destination register is one of the two sources being decoded right now. When this fires, PIPE stalls the fetch and decode stages for exactly one cycle (the instructions already in F and D are held in place, not advanced or re-fetched) and injects a **bubble** — an inert placeholder, not a real instruction — into Execute instead of letting the stalled Decode instruction proceed. One cycle later the load has moved into M, `m_valM` is available combinationally, and the ordinary forwarding chain picks it up for the (still-waiting) consumer. The cost is exactly one wasted cycle per load/use pair, confirmed below by direct simulation. For a straight-line program of $n$ instructions with $s$ load/use stalls and no control hazards, the five-stage pipeline needs

$$\text{cycles} = n + 4 + s$$

cycles in total — four cycles to fill the pipe plus one per instruction, plus one extra per stall.

sections.heading: Pipeline Control Logic and the ret / Load-Use Interaction
sections.body:
The stall and bubble signals are combinational logic over the `icode`, destination and source fields already sitting in the pipeline registers, so the resulting action takes effect at the start of the *next* cycle. Besides the load/use case, PIPE must also hold `F` while a `ret` instruction drains through D, E and M (so that the correct return address, not a speculatively fetched successor, is used), and it must bubble D and E for one cycle on a mispredicted conditional jump. The CENG331 slides' *Pipeline Summary* states the cost of each case plainly: a load/use hazard wastes 1 cycle, a mispredicted branch wastes 2, and a draining `ret` wastes 3 — all absorbed by forwarding except these specific cases.

The first version of the control logic in the lecture slides defines

```text
bool D_bubble =
    (E_icode == IJXX && !e_Cnd) ||               # mispredicted branch
    IRET in { D_icode, E_icode, M_icode };       # ret draining through the pipe
```

This has a bug: when a load into `%rsp` (e.g. `mrmovq (%rbx),%rsp`) is immediately followed by `ret`, the load/use condition on `D_stall` and the `ret` condition on `D_bubble` can both become true for pipeline register D *on the same cycle* — asking the same register to stall and bubble at once, which the simulator reports as a `PIP` (pipeline error) status. CENG331's corrected version, matching both the lab's `pipe-1w.hcl` and `pipe-full.hcl`, gives the load/use condition priority by excluding it from the `ret` term:

```text
bool D_bubble =
    (E_icode == IJXX && !e_Cnd) ||
    ( !(E_icode in { IMRMOVQ, IPOPQ } && E_dstM in { d_srcA, d_srcB }) &&
      IRET in { D_icode, E_icode, M_icode } );
```

With this fix, a `ret` that is itself the victim of a load/use hazard (its implicit source register is `%rsp`) is simply held in Decode for the extra cycle the hazard requires, instead of being bubbled at the same time — exactly the "load/use hazard should get priority" rule the slides state outright.

sections.heading: Engineering Notes: Beyond PIPE
sections.body:
PIPE's stall-or-forward choice is itself a design trade-off, not the only option. A homework variant of the simulator, `pipe-lf.hcl`, adds a bypass path (CS:APP's Figure 4.70, the "Fwd A" block) from the raw memory-read output directly into the `valA` field of pipeline register M, letting one specific form of the load/use dependency be resolved by an extra forwarding path instead of a stall — at the cost of a new comparator and mux rather than a lost cycle. The lab's `README` lists several other single-feature variants built the same way: `pipe-nobypass.hcl` removes all forwarding (every RAW hazard stalls, not just load/use) and `pipe-1w.hcl` restricts the register file to a single write port, which reopens the same `D_bubble` priority question for a second pair of simultaneously-writing instructions.

The same forward-or-stall decision appears, scaled up, in real processors. A compiler's instruction scheduler (GCC's or LLVM's) reorders independent instructions between a load and its first use specifically so that by the time the use executes, the load's latency has already elapsed — the software analogue of PIPE's stall, paid at compile time instead of run time. Out-of-order superscalar x86-64 cores generalize the idea further: instead of one fixed forwarding chain of three stages, a reservation station or scheduler broadcasts a completed result to every waiting consumer the cycle it becomes available, and independent instructions already in flight fill in for an instruction that has to wait — the same cause (RAW hazard on a load) but a very different, dynamically scheduled fix. The RISC-V pipeline in Patterson & Hennessy is architecturally the closest relative: the same five stages, the same E/M/W forwarding chain, and the same one-cycle load/use stall when forwarding cannot reach back in time.

code.caption: Stage-occupancy simulator for the classic CS:APP load/use sequence; detects the hazard and models the stall+bubble, verified by compiling and running it.

worked_example.problem:
Trace this Y86-64 fragment through PIPE's five stages, cycle by cycle, assuming all branches/forwarding work as described above (registers: `%rdx`=0, `%rcx`=1, `%rax`=2, `%rbx`=3):

```text
0x000  irmovq $128,%rdx
0x00a  irmovq $3,%rcx
0x014  rmmovq %rcx,0(%rdx)
0x01e  irmovq $10,%rbx
0x028  mrmovq 0(%rdx),%rax
0x032  addq   %rbx,%rax
0x034  halt
```

Identify every register dependency, say whether each is resolved by forwarding or requires a stall, and give the total number of cycles until `halt` reaches Write-back.
worked_example.solution:
Number the instructions i0–i6 in program order. Running the detection rule `E_icode in {IMRMOVQ, IPOPQ} && E_dstM in {d_srcA, d_srcB}` cycle by cycle (verified by compiling and running the `code` listing above) gives:

| Cycle | F | D | E | M | W | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | i0 | – | – | – | – | |
| 2 | i1 | i0 | – | – | – | |
| 3 | i2 | i1 | i0 | – | – | |
| 4 | i3 | i2 | i1 | i0 | – | |
| 5 | i4 | i3 | i2 | i1 | i0 | |
| 6 | i5 | i4 | i3 | i2 | i1 | |
| 7 | i6 | i5 | i4 | i3 | i2 | hazard detected: E=i4 (load), D=i5 needs `%rax` |
| 8 | i6 | i5 | bubble | i4 | i3 | D held, E bubbled |
| 9 | – | i6 | i5 | bubble | i4 | i5 finally executes |
| 10 | – | – | i6 | i5 | bubble | |
| 11 | – | – | bubble | i6 | i5 | |
| 12 | – | – | – | bubble | i6 | `halt` reaches W: **12 cycles total** |

Three register dependencies occur, and each is resolved differently:

- **i2 (`rmmovq %rcx,0(%rdx)`) in D at cycle 3.** Its first source, `%rcx`, matches `e_dstE` of i1 (in E) → forwarded as `e_valE`. Its second source, `%rdx`, matches `M_dstE` of i0 (in M) → forwarded as `M_valE`. Both resolved the same cycle, no stall — this is the ordinary case forwarding exists for.
- **i5 (`addq %rbx,%rax`) in D at cycle 7.** Source `%rbx` matches `M_dstE` of i3 (in M) → forwards fine. Source `%rax`, however, would need to match a destination of i4, which is in E and is a load (`E_dstM = %rax`, `E_dstE = RNONE`): no E/M/W match exists yet, so `load_use_hazard` is true. PIPE stalls `F` and `D`, bubbles `E`.
- **Same i5, now in D at cycle 8.** `%rbx`'s producer (i3) has moved on to W, so it now forwards as `W_valE`. `%rax`'s producer (i4) has moved into M, where `m_valM` — the value just read from memory this very cycle — is available and matches `M_dstM`, so `%rax` forwards as `m_valM`. Both operands are now resolved and i5 proceeds into E at cycle 9.

Using the cycle formula from the "Load/Use Hazard" section with $n = 7$ instructions and $s = 1$ stall: $7 + 4 + 1 = 12$, matching the trace exactly.

pitfalls: **Treating forwarding sources as unordered.** If two in-flight producers (say one in E, one in M) both target the same register, the one closer to Decode (E) is the more recent in program order and must win; picking the other silently uses a value that is about to be overwritten.

**Confusing `e_valE` with a memory value.** Only an ALU-style result is available combinationally straight out of Execute (`e_valE`). A load's data does not exist until the Memory stage (`m_valM`); there is no `e_valM` signal, which is precisely why the load/use case needs a stall.

**Treating stall and bubble as the same action.** A stall holds an instruction in place for an extra cycle; a bubble discards whatever would have advanced into a stage and replaces it with an inert placeholder. Load/use hazards need both at once, in different pipeline registers.

**Letting independent stall/bubble conditions collide.** Writing the `ret`-draining condition without excluding the load/use case (the original `D_bubble` formula) lets both `D_stall` and `D_bubble` fire for the same register on the same cycle — a `PIP` pipeline-error status, not a silently wrong answer, but still a bug.

**Assuming forwarding fixes every RAW hazard.** It only works when the producer's value already exists by the time the consumer reaches Decode. Load/use is the one case in the base ISA where the value simply isn't computed yet.

**Porting the stall-or-forward intuition directly to a superscalar CPU.** Real out-of-order cores broadcast results to many waiting consumers simultaneously and can execute unrelated instructions while one waits, rather than freezing the whole front end for a fixed number of cycles.
applications: **Compiler instruction scheduling.** GCC and LLVM reorder independent instructions between a load and its first use so the load's latency has elapsed by the time the value is needed — the compile-time analogue of why PIPE needs a stall at all.

**RISC-V's classroom pipeline (Patterson & Hennessy).** Uses the same five stages, the same E/M/W forwarding chain into Decode, and the same one-cycle load/use stall, making it PIPE's closest architectural relative.

**Out-of-order superscalar x86-64 cores.** Generalize forwarding into a broadcast network: a completed result (from a reservation station or physical register) is forwarded the cycle it is ready to every instruction waiting on it, and unrelated instructions can execute in the meantime instead of stalling the whole pipeline.

**CS:APP's own `pipe-lf.hcl` lab variant.** Adds an extra bypass path from the memory stage's raw output into pipeline register M's `valA` field, trading a stall for one more forwarding path — a direct, hands-on example of the stall/forward trade-off.

**Procedure-return handling.** The same combinational-control-with-priority discipline used to fix the `ret`/load-use interaction (Combination B) generalizes to how real pipelines order multiple simultaneous special conditions (exceptions, mispredicts, returns) without letting any two control signals contradict each other.
exam_focus: METU's CENG331 Final 2018 (Q3) gave a PIPE+ code sequence containing `mrmovq (%rbx),%rsp` immediately followed by `popq %rax` plus a taken `jne`, and asked students to name each data and control hazard, the specific registers/instructions involved, and how PIPE+ resolves them — exactly the load-into-a-register-then-use pattern this card analyzes.

The CENG331 PIPE lab (`simguide`) has students single-step the simulator through this exact `mrmovq`/`addq` sequence and read the inserted bubble directly off the Execute stage's status display, confirming by observation that "it acts like a nop instruction."

The lecture slides' Pipeline Summary is the course's own reference numbers for this topic: 1 stall cycle for load/use, 2 wasted cycles for a mispredicted branch, 3 wasted cycles for a draining `ret` — a form that shows up directly in short-answer exam questions.

self_check.question: Why can't PIPE's forwarding logic resolve a load/use hazard the same way it resolves an ALU-to-ALU RAW hazard, and what does PIPE do instead?
self_check.answer: Forwarding routes a value from a pipeline register (or a stage's real-time output) directly into Decode the same cycle it would otherwise be read from the register file. An ALU result (`e_valE`) is already computed combinationally the moment its producer reaches Execute, so it can be forwarded with zero delay. A load's result, however, does not exist until the memory system responds during the producer's Memory stage — one cycle *after* the dependent instruction would need it in Decode. Forwarding a value before it has been computed is impossible, so PIPE instead stalls the dependent instruction in Fetch and Decode for one cycle and injects a bubble into Execute; once the load reaches Memory, the now-available value is forwarded from there (`m_valM`) to the still-waiting consumer.

self_check.question: For the instruction sequence `irmovq $128,%rdx; irmovq $3,%rcx; rmmovq %rcx,0(%rdx); irmovq $10,%rbx; mrmovq 0(%rdx),%rax; addq %rbx,%rax; halt`, how many cycles does PIPE take, and how many would a hypothetical non-forwarding variant (stalling on every RAW hazard, not just load/use, until the producer reaches Write-back) take?
self_check.answer: With forwarding, PIPE takes 12 cycles: 7 instructions need $7+4=11$ cycles to fill and drain the pipe, plus 1 stall cycle for the single load/use hazard between `mrmovq` and `addq` (verified by the worked example and the accompanying simulation). Without any forwarding, every one of the three RAW dependencies in the program (`%rcx` and `%rdx` into `rmmovq`; `%rbx` and `%rax` into `addq`) would have to wait until its producer finished Write-back before the consumer could even enter Decode, re-stalling the same instruction multiple times; simulating that rule on this program (stall D and F whenever a source register matches a destination still in E, M, or W) gives 17 cycles — 5 more, a 42% increase for a 7-instruction program. The gap would grow roughly linearly with how often adjacent instructions depend on each other.

self_check.question: The original `D_bubble` formula ORs a mispredicted-branch term with a plain `ret`-draining term. Construct a short instruction sequence that exposes the bug this causes, and explain exactly how the corrected formula fixes it.
self_check.answer: Take `mrmovq (%rbx),%rsp` followed immediately by `ret`. Y86-64's `ret` reads its return address from the memory location `%rsp` points to, so it implicitly sources `%rsp` — meaning when `mrmovq (%rbx),%rsp` sits in E and `ret` sits in D, the load/use detection condition `E_icode in {IMRMOVQ, IPOPQ} && E_dstM in {d_srcA, d_srcB}` is true (this is 'Combination B'). At the very same cycle, `IRET in {D_icode, E_icode, M_icode}` is also true, since `ret` is sitting in D. The original `D_bubble` formula has no awareness of the first condition, so it unconditionally asserts a bubble for D on the `ret` term while `D_stall` (driven solely by the load/use condition) simultaneously asserts a stall for the same pipeline register — contradictory signals that the simulator reports as a `PIP` error. The corrected formula ANDs the `ret` term with the negation of the load/use condition, so that when both are true, only the stall fires: `ret` is simply held in Decode for the one extra cycle the load/use hazard already requires, and no bubble is asserted until the hazard clears.

key_points: RAW data hazards occur when Decode needs a register value an in-flight producer hasn't written back yet.
Forwarding feeds valE/valM from E, M and W into Decode; the stage closest to Decode wins on a tie.
Load/use hazard: a load's value isn't ready until Memory, one stage later than Decode needs it.
Fix: stall F and D for one cycle, bubble E, then forward the value once it reaches Memory.
Unordered stall/bubble logic can collide: a ret reading %rsp during a load/use hazard needs priority rules.
Course reference costs: load/use = 1 stall cycle, mispredicted branch = 2, draining ret = 3.
tagline: PIPE forwards valE/valM from E, M and W into Decode for free, except load/use, which costs exactly one stall cycle and a bubble.
tldr: PIPE resolves almost every read-after-write hazard by **forwarding** the producer's value from the Execute, Memory or Write-back pipeline register directly into Decode, with priority given to whichever stage is closest to Decode. The one case forwarding cannot reach is the **load/use hazard**, where a loaded value isn't available until the Memory stage — one cycle too late — so PIPE instead **stalls** Fetch and Decode for a cycle and injects a **bubble** into Execute. Getting the control logic for this right is subtler than it looks: an unguarded `ret`-draining condition can collide with a simultaneous load/use hazard unless one is given explicit priority over the other.
